data.summary: Three LK tasks (LK-hook-snapshot, LK-observed-globs, LK-sg-events) each add a config section; registering one needs edits to the shared config/__init__.py and config/_core.py (and LK-hook-snapshot and LK-observed-globs both create config_sections/locks.py), so claims refuse each other. A section registry by convention (auto-discover config_sections/*.py) would remove the shared files.
data.title: New config section forces a lease on ddflow/config/__init__.py and _core.py: parallel tasks adding [locks]/[handoff] block each other

data.body:
Fixes bug Bd7117525b9: Three LK tasks (LK-hook-snapshot, LK-observed-globs, LK-sg-events) each add a config section; registering one needs edits to the shared config/__init__.py and config/_core.py (and LK-hook-snapshot and LK-observed-globs both create config_sections/locks.py), so claims refuse each other. A section registry by convention (auto-discover config_sections/*.py) would remove the shared files. Found on LK-hook-snapshot.

Write the regression test first and watch it FAIL on the unfixed code; then `ddflow complete fix-Bd7117525b9 --regression-test <test>` closes the bug with the task (or `ddflow bug fixed Bd7117525b9 --regression-test <test>` first).

data.claim: A JSON snapshot of live leases updated incrementally on lease events is read in well under 30 ms and fails open with a notice when stale or missing
data.falsifier: p95 of the hook read over 200 calls >= 30 ms, or a stale snapshot passes silently
data.mechanism: The log fold costs 2.5 s read + 1.1 s fold (3.7 s measured); a 60-lease JSON file is one small read
data.probe: pytest tests/test_lease_snapshot.py
data.probe_output: 13 passed; test_hook_read_budget_p95_under_30_ms and test_hook_fails_open_and_says_so_when_unusable pass; fold timing 2.56s+1.08s on this repo
data.question: Can a per-edit hook decide lease coverage from a local snapshot under 30 ms p95 instead of folding the 108 MB log?

evidence.note: research note CONFIRMED: fold 2.56s+1.08s measured; snapshot read p95 asserted <30ms in tests/test_lease_snapshot.py (13 passed)

r-small-files (all files <30000 bytes), r-reuse-core (LocalStore, APPEND_HOOKS, config knob registry reused), r-everything-configurable ([locks].snapshot, snapshot_max_age_s), r-no-shell (notices name ddflow heartbeat / ddflow_heartbeat), r-adapters (no new external dependency)

chunk_findings.detail: `read()` does not reject non-finite numeric fields. Python's `json.loads` accepts `NaN` and `Infinity` by default, so a snapshot such as `{"schema":1,"data":{"leases":{},"written_at":NaN,"max_age_s":60}}` gets `float(data["written_at"]) == nan`, then `age` is `nan`; `nan > limit` is false, so the stale check is bypassed and the function returns `status="ok"` forever. That is the silent-pass behavior the module says it exists to avoid. With `{"written_at":-Infinity,"max_age_s":60}` the stale branch is taken and `int(age)` raises an uncaught `OverflowError`; `{"max_age_s":Infinity}` also raises `OverflowError` inside `int(...)` because the except list omits `OverflowError`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce/hooksnap.py:81

chunk_findings.detail: `read()` validates only that `data["leases"]` is a dict, then blindly iterates `data.get("shared", [])` and `data.get("new_files", [])`. If the file contains `{"schema":1,"data":{"leases":{},"written_at":0,"max_age_s":60,"shared":null}}`, `data.get("shared", [])` returns `None` because the key exists, and line 92 raises `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not iterable`. The same happens for `new_files: null` or a non-iterable scalar. Instead of returning an `UNREADABLE` snapshot and failing open with the promised next-call sentence, the per-edit hook can crash. If `shared` is a string such as `"src/**"`, it is silently converted to one-character globs `["s","r","c",...]`, producing wrong allow/deny decisions.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce/hooksnap.py:92

chunk_findings.detail: `read()` silently drops malformed lease entries instead of reporting the snapshot as unreadable. For input `{"schema":1,"data":{"leases":{"other-lane":"corrupt"},"written_at":0,"max_age_s":60}}`, the leases table is a dict, so the file passes validation, but the dict comprehension filters out the non-dict value and returns `Snapshot(status="ok", leases={})`. A hook checking whether another lane holds a claim now sees a trustworthy snapshot with no leases and may allow a conflicting write. This directly violates the stated contract that a torn snapshot must be reported and never read as "no leases".
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce/hooksnap.py:91

chunk_findings.detail: `Snapshot.live_for()` can raise on lease entries that `read()` accepted. For example, `{"schema":1,"data":{"leases":{"a":{"holder":"me","renewed_at":1,"ttl_s":"nope"}},"written_at":0,"max_age_s":60}}` returns an `OK` snapshot from `read()`, but calling `snap.live_for("me", 2)` raises `ValueError` from `int("nope")`. If `ttl_s` is `Infinity`, `int(...)` raises `OverflowError`. A malformed but structurally accepted snapshot can therefore crash the hook instead of producing a non-OK `Snapshot` that fails open.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce/hooksnap.py:53

chunk_findings.detail: This module hardcodes the `.ddflow/local/lease-snapshot.json` layout and calls `time.time()` and `Path.read_text()` directly instead of using a port in `ddflow/adapters`. Per [r-adapters], filesystem layout and clocks are external dependencies that should go through a port with one implementation; here the layout is duplicated with the writer and cannot be swapped or faked without monkeypatching the filesystem/time.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce/hooksnap.py:57

chunk_findings.detail: The writer treats a successful incremental write as proof that the snapshot is current, but it silently swallows any earlier snapshot-update failure and never records an “unavailable” state. `appended` catches all exceptions and ignores `apply()` returning false; if the previous file is still present and within `max_age_s`, the hook will read it as fresh even though it is missing the event whose update failed. For example, suppose the snapshot is fresh at `t=0` and contains no lease on `src/**`. At `t=1` a `lease.acquired` event for item `T2` with glob `src/**` is appended, but the snapshot update fails (disk full, permission error, config load error, or any transient error other than `StoreUnreadable`). `appended` suppresses the failure and leaves the old snapshot in place. At `t=2` a hook reads that old file, sees `written_at` still fresh, sees no `T2` lease, and allows an edit to `src/**` instead of failing open to the commit-time check. The problem is made worse because any later watched event—even one that changes no lease, such as an unrelated `phase.removed`—can call `apply()`, see `cur["leases"]` is a dict, write `written_at=now`, and make the stale/incomplete snapshot appear fresh again. This violates the stated “stale or missing snapshot fails open / never a silent pass” contract.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/snapshot.py:appended/apply

chunk_findings.detail: The change replaces the current-config call `list(shared_globs(cfg))` with `snap.shared`, so the hook trusts the shared globs stored in the last lease snapshot. The snapshot is described as being refreshed only on lease acquire/renew/release/expire, not when `[locks]` config changes. If the config is changed after the last lease event while the snapshot is still within `snapshot_max_age_s`, `hooksnap.read` can return `OK` with stale shared globs. For example, with no shared globs originally, a lease event writes a snapshot; then the operator adds `docs/**` to `[locks] shared_globs`; a lane with no live lease writes `docs/x.md`. `_mine` returns `shared=[]`, `mine=[]`, and `check` returns REFUSE even though the current config makes the write shared/allowed. This is a false refusal caused by config-stale snapshot data that is not detected as stale.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/swarm/lanehooks_check.py:_mine

chunk_findings.detail: When the snapshot is unusable, the hook returns `0, f"{why} The call is allowed (not checked here)."`. The intent/conformance requires every refusal or notice to name the exact next call in CLI and MCP form, and the stale/missing-snapshot path is supposed to fail open to the commit-time check and say so. This message only says “not checked here”; it does not tell the caller which commit-time check will run or the exact next CLI/MCP call, so the required next step is not discoverable. [r-tell-dont-discover]
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/swarm/lanehooks_check.py:check

chunk_findings.detail: The test does not measure the hook path whose budget the intent specifies. It calls the private helper `CK._mine` 200 times in a warm loop, while the hook entry point exercised elsewhere in the same file is `CK.verdict`. If `CK.verdict` adds any cost beyond `_mine` (for example, another snapshot read, path normalization, shared/new-file handling, or building the refusal/fail-open message), or if a fresh per-edit hook process has a cold-start cost above 30 ms, the p95 of these warm in-process `_mine` calls can still pass. Thus the actual hook can violate the stated 30 ms p95 budget and this test will not catch it.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_lease_snapshot.py:test_hook_read_budget_p95_under_30_ms

chunk_findings.detail: The test simulates concurrent writers with threads in one process and a shared `EventLog` object. The real concurrent writers are separate CLI/hook processes. If `S.apply` serializes snapshot updates only with an in-process mechanism such as a `threading.Lock` (or relies on shared in-memory state), this test passes because the threads are serialized inside one process, but two OS processes can still read the same old snapshot, compute the same next generation, and atomically replace each other's file, losing lease entries and generation increments. The test therefore does not prove the required cross-process atomicity.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_lease_snapshot.py:test_concurrent_writers_all_land

chunk_findings.detail: The snapshot fixture never writes or tests the caller identity map required by the intent, and the hook tests call with a caller string identical to the lease holder. If `S._doc` drops the identities field or `CK.verdict` ignores it, every test still passes because no test maps a caller identity (for example `agent-1`) to a holder. A broken identity map would make real hooks refuse allowed callers or allow the wrong ones, yet this test suite would give a false pass.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_lease_snapshot.py:_write/test_hook_judges_from_a_fresh_snapshot

chunk_findings.detail: The doc string for `snapshot_max_age_s` tells operators to configure `[lease].renew_log_min_s`, but the config section in this file is `locks` (the same doc and its sibling use `locks.snapshot`, `DDFLOW_LOCKS_*`, `ddflow config locks.snapshot*`). An operator who follows this doc, e.g. `ddflow config lease.renew_log_min_s 60`, gets an unknown section/key, and the documented staleness behavior cannot be adjusted at the stated path.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/locks.py:50

chunk_findings.detail: The fallback `ttl_s` is hardcoded as `1800` when a `lease.acquired` event’s `data` omits `ttl_s` (the very path this fallback exists for), and the `lease.renewed` branch never updates `ttl_s`. Given a configured lease TTL of e.g. `7200` and an acquire event with `{"holder": "a", "globs": [...], "at": 1700000000}`, the snapshot records `ttl_s: 1800`; after 30 minutes the hook derives an expired lease from a still-valid one. The correct default/updated value should come from config, not a fixed number.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/snapshot.py:55 `_entry`

chunk_findings.detail: A snapshot that misses an event is only healed when `cur` is missing or `cur["leases"]` is not a dict. The `before`/`after` log positions are ignored, no log position is recorded, and `appended` suppresses a non-`StoreUnreadable` update failure. Concrete failure: the snapshot says item X is held; `lease.released` for X is appended but the snapshot write fails (e.g. `OSError`) or the process dies before the write; the next `lease.acquired` for Y sees a valid `cur`, applies only Y, and writes a fresh `written_at`. The snapshot now still says X is held but is not “stale” by age, so a hook will trust it rather than fail open to the commit-time check, despite the log having released X.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/snapshot.py:132-138 `apply` step / 154 `appended`

chunk_findings.detail: `_mine` now takes `shared` from the snapshot (`return globs, snap.shared`) instead of computing it fresh from `Config.load(repo)`/`shared_globs(cfg)`. The snapshot is only updated on lease acquire/renew/release/expire, but shared globs are configuration and can change without any lease event. Concrete case: a live lease for `src/**` exists and the snapshot was written with `shared=[]`; the repo then switches branch or edits config so current `[locks].shared=["docs/**"]`; before any lease event writes a new snapshot, `lanehooks_check` is called for a write to `docs/new.md`. `shared` is still `[]`, the path is not in `mine+shared`, and `check` returns `REFUSE`, even though the current commit-time config would allow the write. The old code did not have this stale-config window because it read the current config on every call.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/swarm/lanehooks_check.py:_mine

chunk_findings.detail: The new fallback notice is `return 0, f"{why} The call is allowed (not checked here)."`. This is a notice to the caller, but it does not name the exact next call in CLI and MCP form, which the conformance requirement in the intent says every refusal and notice must do [D-lock-lifecycle-answers]. A stale/torn/missing snapshot therefore allows the call while leaving the caller without the required actionable next command.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/swarm/lanehooks_check.py:check fallback

chunk_findings.detail: `read` reads the JSON file with `p.read_text("utf-8")` without any file locking or atomic checking against torn writes. If a concurrent writer in `ddflow/services/leases/snapshot.py` is in the middle of writing the `.ddflow/local/lease-snapshot.json` file (e.g., truncating or partially writing), `json.loads` will raise a `ValueError` (JSONDecodeError), causing `read` to catch it and return an `UNREADABLE` status. However, if a write is torn such that `json.loads` succeeds partially or if an OS exception occurs mid-write, unexpected structures or corrupted data can bypass validation or crash the hook, violating the concurrency and torn file requirement explicitly requested in the intent ("Tests incl. concurrent writers, torn file, stale").
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce/hooksnap.py:65

chunk_findings.detail: `read` returns `status=OK` after only checking that `data["leases"]` is a dict, then silently drops every lease entry whose value is not a dict. For example, a snapshot containing `{"schema":1,"data":{"leases":{"lease-1":null,"lease-2":{"holder":"a","renewed_at":10,"ttl_s":30}},"written_at":10,"max_age_s":100}}` makes `read(repo, now=10)` return OK with only `lease-2`; if `lease-1` was the lease covering the edited file or held by another lane, the hook sees no lease and can allow the edit, exactly the “never read as no leases” case the docstring forbids. A lease value that is a dict but has `ttl_s:null` is also accepted as OK and makes `Snapshot.live_for` raise `TypeError` at line 51 instead of producing a bad-status snapshot.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce/hooksnap.py:89

chunk_findings.detail: `read` can raise an exception instead of returning `UNREADABLE` when `shared` or `new_files` is present but not iterable. `data.get("shared", [])` returns `None` when the key exists with a null value, so the comprehension at line 90 iterates `None`; for example, `{"schema":1,"data":{"leases":{},"written_at":10,"max_age_s":100,"shared":null}}` with `read(repo, now=10)` raises `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not iterable` (same for `"new_files":null`), so the hook cannot print the documented fail-open note. A string such as `"shared":"src/**"` is also silently split into single-character globs rather than rejected.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce/hooksnap.py:90

chunk_findings.detail: The snapshot can become fresh but incomplete after a failed or ignored update. `apply` only handles `StoreUnreadable`; any other write failure is swallowed by `appended` (`contextlib.suppress(Exception)`), and even a successful `store.update` refreshes `written_at`/`generation` through `_doc` when `project` did nothing (for example, a `lease.renewed` for a subject absent from a valid snapshot returns at line 69). Given a valid snapshot `{"generation": 1, "written_at": now-10, "max_age_s": 300, "leases": {}}`, a failed `lease.acquired` for item `A` leaves that file unchanged; a later successful `lease.acquired` for unrelated item `B` writes `written_at=now` while still missing `A`. The hook sees a fresh snapshot, treats `A` as unleased, and passes silently instead of reporting the snapshot unavailable and falling back to the commit-time check.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/snapshot.py:144 (apply/appended)

chunk_findings.detail: Terminal item events are dropped only when the event holder matches the snapshot holder. For `item.completed`, `item.abandoned`, or removed subjects, the lease should disappear regardless of who emitted the terminal event. Given a snapshot entry `leases["item-1"] = {"holder": "agentA", ...}` and an `item.completed` event with `subject="item-1"` and `data={"holder": "agentB"}`, line 79 fails the holder comparison and leaves the lease in place. A rebuild via `from_log` would skip the terminal item, so the incremental snapshot and the authoritative log view diverge; the hook can see a live lease for an already completed item.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/snapshot.py:79 (project)

chunk_findings.detail: The writer calls `time.time()` directly instead of using a clock port/adapter. This bypasses the project's adapter rule for clocks [r-adapters] and makes the snapshot’s `written_at` and lease freshness depend on the real system clock even in tests or environments that install a controlled clock adapter.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/snapshot.py:135 (step)

chunk_findings.detail: The changed `_mine` now returns `snap.shared` directly from the snapshot file, and the hook uses that list to decide whether a write is allowed. The snapshot is only refreshed on lease events, but the shared-glob configuration can change without any lease event, so the snapshot can remain “OK” and within `snapshot_max_age_s` while its `shared` list is stale. Example: `[locks].snapshot_max_age_s` is 3600, a lane holds a lease on `src/a.py`, and the snapshot was written when the config had `shared_globs = ["shared/**"]`. The operator edits the config to remove `shared/**`, but no lease is acquired, renewed, released, or expired. The hook reads the fresh snapshot, still sees `shared/**`, and allows the lane to edit `shared/secret.txt`; the current config would not permit that shared write, so the per-edit hook passes a call that the commit-time check would refuse. The same staleness can falsely refuse a newly added shared glob. This makes the hook’s allow decision depend on stale configured shared globs [r-everything-configurable].
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/swarm/lanehooks_check.py:_mine

chunk_findings.detail: The test claims to assert the hook’s 30 ms p95 budget, but it times only the private helper `CK._mine`, not the hook entry point used elsewhere in the same file (`CK.verdict`). If `CK.verdict` still performs any expensive work before or after calling `_mine`—for example, folding the event log or rebuilding shared/new-file globs from the log, the very 3.7 s cost this change is meant to avoid—the measured `_mine` calls can still be well under 30 ms and the test passes while the actual hook violates the budget. The budget must be measured on the hook/public verdict path, not only an internal helper.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_lease_snapshot.py:test_hook_read_budget_p95_under_30_ms

chunk_findings.detail: The knob doc tells users the heartbeat rewrite cadence is controlled by `[lease].renew_log_min_s`, but this same doc and file configure the `locks` section (`ddflow config locks.snapshot_max_age_s ...`, file `ddflow/config_sections/locks.py`). A user following the doc sets a wrong or nonexistent `lease` section, so the intended renewal cadence is not changed and the snapshot can go stale earlier than expected, making the write hook fall back to the commit-time check unexpectedly. The reference should be `[locks].renew_log_min_s`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/locks.py:snapshot_max_age_s

chunk_findings.detail: The new reader reaches the real filesystem and clock directly (`Path.read_text`, `time.time`) instead of going through a port in `ddflow/adapters`. [r-adapters] requires filesystem layout and clocks to be behind one swappable/fakeable adapter; this implementation cannot be swapped or tested with a fake and bypasses the project rule.
chunk_findings.title: [r-adapters] ddflow/services/enforce/hooksnap.py:read

chunk_findings.detail: `read` does not validate the contents of each lease entry or the `shared`/`new_files` values; it silently drops any lease whose value is not a dict and coerces non-list glob values. A parseable snapshot such as `{"schema":1,"data":{"written_at":1234567890.0,"max_age_s":10,"generation":1,"grace_s":0,"leases":{"lease-a":"bad"},"shared":[],"new_files":[]}}` returns `Snapshot(status=OK, leases={})`, so an untrustworthy snapshot is treated as trustworthy and the held lease disappears; a lease dict with `"renewed_at":"not-a-number"` would also make `live_for` raise `ValueError` after `read` returned `OK`, crashing the hook instead of failing open.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce/hooksnap.py:read

chunk_findings.detail: When a previous update fails in a way that does **not** raise `StoreUnreadable` but leaves the old snapshot file readable (for example a write/OSError during `store.update`, or any non-`StoreUnreadable` exception raised by `step`), the next successful watched event will not rebuild from the log. The `ok` check at `isinstance(cur, dict) and isinstance(cur.get("leases"), dict)` passes, so it only projects that next event onto the old, already-stale in-memory state and then writes `written_at` to the current time via `_doc`. The missed events are never repaired, yet the file no longer ages out, so the hook treats it as fresh and will not fail open. Concrete failure: `lease.released` for item X is appended and the snapshot write fails leaving the old snapshot that still lists X; later `lease.acquired` for item Y succeeds and writes a fresh snapshot that still falsely lists X as held.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/snapshot.py:apply (step function)

chunk_findings.detail: The project rule makes clocks an adapter dependency, but this file calls `time.time()` directly in `apply.step` (it is also used indirectly for `written_at` and `from_log`). This bypasses the clock port and prevents tests or alternative clock implementations from controlling time, directly affecting stale-age and lease-expiry behavior.
chunk_findings.title: [r-adapters] ddflow/services/leases/snapshot.py:131

chunk_findings.detail: When the lease snapshot is missing, stale, torn, or newer, `check` returns exit code `0` with only `f"{why} The call is allowed (not checked here)."` The project's CONFORMANCE requirement says a hook that could not run is recorded unavailable and fails open to the commit-time check, never passed. Exit `0` is what the harness treats as a successful/passed hook, and the code does not record the snapshot as unavailable, so a missing `.ddflow/local/lease-snapshot.json` (e.g., a freshly cloned repo with no lease event yet) is marked as a pass, not as “unavailable, commit-time check”; the message also does not name the exact next CLI and MCP call the requirement demands.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/swarm/lanehooks_check.py:95

chunk_findings.detail: A hard real-time p95 assertion in a unit test is environment-dependent. On a loaded CI runner, antivirus scan, or a network-backed temp filesystem, `CK._mine` can exceed 30 ms even with a correct implementation because OS scheduling/IO outliers are outside the code’s control. The suite then fails spuriously; 200 in-process samples do not make the assertion deterministic.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_lease_snapshot.py:test_hook_read_budget_p95_under_30_ms

chunk_findings.detail: The test ignores the exit status of `run_cli(repo, "claim", "T1")`. If `locks.snapshot = false` makes the claim fail before it would write the snapshot, `H.path_of(repo).exists()` is still false and the test passes. The property to verify is that a *successful* claim writes nothing; without asserting claim success, this test can pass when the feature is broken.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_lease_snapshot.py:test_snapshot_off_writes_nothing

chunk_findings.detail: The concurrency test only spawns threads inside one process. The operational hazard is two separate `ddflow` processes writing the same repository snapshot concurrently. An implementation that protects its read-modify-write with only a `threading.Lock` would pass this test, while two parallel CLI processes could still race and lose one or more lease updates. The test does not exercise the cross-process interleaving needed to establish the claimed safety.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_lease_snapshot.py:test_concurrent_writers_all_land

chunk_findings.detail: `read()` in `hooksnap.py` reads a JSON file via `json.loads(p.read_text("utf-8"))` without any file locking or atomic rename consideration, while the writer in `ddflow/services/leases/snapshot.py` (part 2) writes to the same file. When a reader attempts to read the file concurrently while the writer is performing a partial write or temp-file rename, `json.loads` raises a `json.JSONDecodeError` (`ValueError`), which is caught by `except (OSError, ValueError):` and results in returning an `UNREADABLE` snapshot. According to the architecture intent, "A stale or missing snapshot makes the hook fail open to the commit-time check and say so", but returning `UNREADABLE` instead of treating it as missing or stale causes the hook to crash or fail closed, or drop into incorrect error handling paths because `SnapshotUnusable` expects specific statuses. Furthermore, reading a half-written file due to lack of a robust retry or lock mechanism on the reader side leads to spurious hook failures during concurrent lease operations.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce/hooksnap.py:66

chunk_findings.detail: The module-level registration `if appended not in APPEND_HOOKS: APPEND_HOOKS.append(appended)` mutates a global list upon import. If `ddflow.services.leases.snapshot` is imported multiple times or imported during tests before `APPEND_HOOKS` is initialized or reset, it leads to duplicate hook entries or import-time side effects. More critically, `appended` uses `Config.load(log.root)`, which reads configuration from disk synchronously inside an append hook called during event logging under a log lock; doing filesystem I/O and config parsing on every log append degrades log write performance and can cause re-entrancy issues if configuration loading itself triggers log operations.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/snapshot.py:157

chunk_findings.detail: `read()` does not reject non-finite numeric fields. Python's `json.loads` accepts `NaN` and `Infinity` by default, so a snapshot such as `{"schema":1,"data":{"leases":{},"written_at":NaN,"max_age_s":60}}` gets `float(data["written_at"]) == nan`, then `age` is `nan`; `nan > limit` is false, so the stale check is bypassed and the function returns `status="ok"` forever. That is the silent-pass behavior the module says it exists to avoid. With `{"written_at":-Infinity,"max_age_s":60}` the stale branch is taken and `int(age)` raises an uncaught `OverflowError`; `{"max_age_s":Infinity}` also raises `OverflowError` inside `int(...)` because the except list omits `OverflowError`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce/hooksnap.py:81

chunk_findings.detail: `read()` validates only that `data["leases"]` is a dict, then blindly iterates `data.get("shared", [])` and `data.get("new_files", [])`. If the file contains `{"schema":1,"data":{"leases":{},"written_at":0,"max_age_s":60,"shared":null}}`, `data.get("shared", [])` returns `None` because the key exists, and line 92 raises `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not iterable`. The same happens for `new_files: null` or a non-iterable scalar. Instead of returning an `UNREADABLE` snapshot and failing open with the promised next-call sentence, the per-edit hook can crash. If `shared` is a string such as `"src/**"`, it is silently converted to one-character globs `["s","r","c",...]`, producing wrong allow/deny decisions.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce/hooksnap.py:92

chunk_findings.detail: `read()` silently drops malformed lease entries instead of reporting the snapshot as unreadable. For input `{"schema":1,"data":{"leases":{"other-lane":"corrupt"},"written_at":0,"max_age_s":60}}`, the leases table is a dict, so the file passes validation, but the dict comprehension filters out the non-dict value and returns `Snapshot(status="ok", leases={})`. A hook checking whether another lane holds a claim now sees a trustworthy snapshot with no leases and may allow a conflicting write. This directly violates the stated contract that a torn snapshot must be reported and never read as "no leases".
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce/hooksnap.py:91

chunk_findings.detail: `Snapshot.live_for()` can raise on lease entries that `read()` accepted. For example, `{"schema":1,"data":{"leases":{"a":{"holder":"me","renewed_at":1,"ttl_s":"nope"}},"written_at":0,"max_age_s":60}}` returns an `OK` snapshot from `read()`, but calling `snap.live_for("me", 2)` raises `ValueError` from `int("nope")`. If `ttl_s` is `Infinity`, `int(...)` raises `OverflowError`. A malformed but structurally accepted snapshot can therefore crash the hook instead of producing a non-OK `Snapshot` that fails open.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce/hooksnap.py:53

chunk_findings.detail: This module hardcodes the `.ddflow/local/lease-snapshot.json` layout and calls `time.time()` and `Path.read_text()` directly instead of using a port in `ddflow/adapters`. Per [r-adapters], filesystem layout and clocks are external dependencies that should go through a port with one implementation; here the layout is duplicated with the writer and cannot be swapped or faked without monkeypatching the filesystem/time.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce/hooksnap.py:57

chunk_findings.detail: The writer treats a successful incremental write as proof that the snapshot is current, but it silently swallows any earlier snapshot-update failure and never records an “unavailable” state. `appended` catches all exceptions and ignores `apply()` returning false; if the previous file is still present and within `max_age_s`, the hook will read it as fresh even though it is missing the event whose update failed. For example, suppose the snapshot is fresh at `t=0` and contains no lease on `src/**`. At `t=1` a `lease.acquired` event for item `T2` with glob `src/**` is appended, but the snapshot update fails (disk full, permission error, config load error, or any transient error other than `StoreUnreadable`). `appended` suppresses the failure and leaves the old snapshot in place. At `t=2` a hook reads that old file, sees `written_at` still fresh, sees no `T2` lease, and allows an edit to `src/**` instead of failing open to the commit-time check. The problem is made worse because any later watched event—even one that changes no lease, such as an unrelated `phase.removed`—can call `apply()`, see `cur["leases"]` is a dict, write `written_at=now`, and make the stale/incomplete snapshot appear fresh again. This violates the stated “stale or missing snapshot fails open / never a silent pass” contract.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/snapshot.py:appended/apply

chunk_findings.detail: The change replaces the current-config call `list(shared_globs(cfg))` with `snap.shared`, so the hook trusts the shared globs stored in the last lease snapshot. The snapshot is described as being refreshed only on lease acquire/renew/release/expire, not when `[locks]` config changes. If the config is changed after the last lease event while the snapshot is still within `snapshot_max_age_s`, `hooksnap.read` can return `OK` with stale shared globs. For example, with no shared globs originally, a lease event writes a snapshot; then the operator adds `docs/**` to `[locks] shared_globs`; a lane with no live lease writes `docs/x.md`. `_mine` returns `shared=[]`, `mine=[]`, and `check` returns REFUSE even though the current config makes the write shared/allowed. This is a false refusal caused by config-stale snapshot data that is not detected as stale.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/swarm/lanehooks_check.py:_mine

chunk_findings.detail: When the snapshot is unusable, the hook returns `0, f"{why} The call is allowed (not checked here)."`. The intent/conformance requires every refusal or notice to name the exact next call in CLI and MCP form, and the stale/missing-snapshot path is supposed to fail open to the commit-time check and say so. This message only says “not checked here”; it does not tell the caller which commit-time check will run or the exact next CLI/MCP call, so the required next step is not discoverable. [r-tell-dont-discover]
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/swarm/lanehooks_check.py:check

chunk_findings.detail: The test does not measure the hook path whose budget the intent specifies. It calls the private helper `CK._mine` 200 times in a warm loop, while the hook entry point exercised elsewhere in the same file is `CK.verdict`. If `CK.verdict` adds any cost beyond `_mine` (for example, another snapshot read, path normalization, shared/new-file handling, or building the refusal/fail-open message), or if a fresh per-edit hook process has a cold-start cost above 30 ms, the p95 of these warm in-process `_mine` calls can still pass. Thus the actual hook can violate the stated 30 ms p95 budget and this test will not catch it.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_lease_snapshot.py:test_hook_read_budget_p95_under_30_ms

chunk_findings.detail: The test simulates concurrent writers with threads in one process and a shared `EventLog` object. The real concurrent writers are separate CLI/hook processes. If `S.apply` serializes snapshot updates only with an in-process mechanism such as a `threading.Lock` (or relies on shared in-memory state), this test passes because the threads are serialized inside one process, but two OS processes can still read the same old snapshot, compute the same next generation, and atomically replace each other's file, losing lease entries and generation increments. The test therefore does not prove the required cross-process atomicity.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_lease_snapshot.py:test_concurrent_writers_all_land

chunk_findings.detail: The snapshot fixture never writes or tests the caller identity map required by the intent, and the hook tests call with a caller string identical to the lease holder. If `S._doc` drops the identities field or `CK.verdict` ignores it, every test still passes because no test maps a caller identity (for example `agent-1`) to a holder. A broken identity map would make real hooks refuse allowed callers or allow the wrong ones, yet this test suite would give a false pass.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_lease_snapshot.py:_write/test_hook_judges_from_a_fresh_snapshot

chunk_findings.detail: The doc string for `snapshot_max_age_s` tells operators to configure `[lease].renew_log_min_s`, but the config section in this file is `locks` (the same doc and its sibling use `locks.snapshot`, `DDFLOW_LOCKS_*`, `ddflow config locks.snapshot*`). An operator who follows this doc, e.g. `ddflow config lease.renew_log_min_s 60`, gets an unknown section/key, and the documented staleness behavior cannot be adjusted at the stated path.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/locks.py:50

chunk_findings.detail: The fallback `ttl_s` is hardcoded as `1800` when a `lease.acquired` event’s `data` omits `ttl_s` (the very path this fallback exists for), and the `lease.renewed` branch never updates `ttl_s`. Given a configured lease TTL of e.g. `7200` and an acquire event with `{"holder": "a", "globs": [...], "at": 1700000000}`, the snapshot records `ttl_s: 1800`; after 30 minutes the hook derives an expired lease from a still-valid one. The correct default/updated value should come from config, not a fixed number.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/snapshot.py:55 `_entry`

chunk_findings.detail: A snapshot that misses an event is only healed when `cur` is missing or `cur["leases"]` is not a dict. The `before`/`after` log positions are ignored, no log position is recorded, and `appended` suppresses a non-`StoreUnreadable` update failure. Concrete failure: the snapshot says item X is held; `lease.released` for X is appended but the snapshot write fails (e.g. `OSError`) or the process dies before the write; the next `lease.acquired` for Y sees a valid `cur`, applies only Y, and writes a fresh `written_at`. The snapshot now still says X is held but is not “stale” by age, so a hook will trust it rather than fail open to the commit-time check, despite the log having released X.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/snapshot.py:132-138 `apply` step / 154 `appended`

chunk_findings.detail: `_mine` now takes `shared` from the snapshot (`return globs, snap.shared`) instead of computing it fresh from `Config.load(repo)`/`shared_globs(cfg)`. The snapshot is only updated on lease acquire/renew/release/expire, but shared globs are configuration and can change without any lease event. Concrete case: a live lease for `src/**` exists and the snapshot was written with `shared=[]`; the repo then switches branch or edits config so current `[locks].shared=["docs/**"]`; before any lease event writes a new snapshot, `lanehooks_check` is called for a write to `docs/new.md`. `shared` is still `[]`, the path is not in `mine+shared`, and `check` returns `REFUSE`, even though the current commit-time config would allow the write. The old code did not have this stale-config window because it read the current config on every call.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/swarm/lanehooks_check.py:_mine

chunk_findings.detail: The new fallback notice is `return 0, f"{why} The call is allowed (not checked here)."`. This is a notice to the caller, but it does not name the exact next call in CLI and MCP form, which the conformance requirement in the intent says every refusal and notice must do [D-lock-lifecycle-answers]. A stale/torn/missing snapshot therefore allows the call while leaving the caller without the required actionable next command.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/swarm/lanehooks_check.py:check fallback

chunk_findings.detail: `read` reads the JSON file with `p.read_text("utf-8")` without any file locking or atomic checking against torn writes. If a concurrent writer in `ddflow/services/leases/snapshot.py` is in the middle of writing the `.ddflow/local/lease-snapshot.json` file (e.g., truncating or partially writing), `json.loads` will raise a `ValueError` (JSONDecodeError), causing `read` to catch it and return an `UNREADABLE` status. However, if a write is torn such that `json.loads` succeeds partially or if an OS exception occurs mid-write, unexpected structures or corrupted data can bypass validation or crash the hook, violating the concurrency and torn file requirement explicitly requested in the intent ("Tests incl. concurrent writers, torn file, stale").
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce/hooksnap.py:65

chunk_findings.detail: `config_stamp()` uses `0` both as the sentinel for “config file absent or `os.stat` failed” and as a possible real `st_mtime_ns` value. Given a snapshot written while `.ddflow/config.toml` was absent (recorded `config_stamp` `[0, 0]`, `shared=[]`), later restoring or creating that file from an archive with epoch mtime (`touch -d @0 .ddflow/config.toml`) containing `[locks] shared=["src/**"]` makes `config_stamp(repo)` return `[0, 0]` again. The reader then sees `stamp == config_stamp(repo)`, returns `status="ok"`, and a hook using `snap.shared` trusts the stale empty list and can allow a conflicting write instead of failing open. The same conflation means an `OSError` while statting config is not recorded as unavailable.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce/hooksnap.py:config_stamp

chunk_findings.detail: `_continues` never verifies the current size of the shard being updated; for the target shard it only checks `marks.get(name, 0) == before` and ignores `size`. Suppose the current snapshot has `marks = {"lease-events.jsonl": 0}`. Process A appends a lease event to that shard with `before=0`; process B appends another lease event to the same shard before A’s snapshot update reads the file, making the current shard size larger. When A calls `_continues`, the target branch sees `marks.get(shard, 0) == before` (`0 == 0`) and returns `True` even though the log has advanced beyond the snapshot. A then applies only its own event and `_doc` writes `marks=_sizes(log)`, recording the current size as if B’s event had been folded. A hook reading that snapshot gets `status="ok"` while missing B’s lease acquire/release; if B’s update never completes (crash, killed hook, etc.), the missing event is permanently masked by the refreshed marks.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/snapshot.py:_continues

chunk_findings.detail: `_continues` treats a current-looking snapshot as usable if `cur["leases"]` is merely a dict, without validating the lease entries themselves. Given a corrupt snapshot such as `{"generation": 1, "written_at": ..., "marks": {...}, "config_stamp": ..., "leases": {"item": "bad"}}` whose marks and config stamp match, `_continues` returns `True` instead of forcing a rebuild from the log. The subsequent incremental `_apply` for `lease.renewed`, `lease.released`, or `lease.expired` dereferences the non-dict lease value (`cur["holder"]` is evaluated as the default argument), raising `TypeError` rather than producing a rebuilt snapshot or an explicit fail-open result. A torn or malformed snapshot should be considered not current and rebuilt, not accepted as exact.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/snapshot.py:_continues

chunk_findings.detail: `apply` performs a read-modify-write without compare-and-swap or post-step revalidation. `_continues` is checked only on the `cur` value that `store.update` read before `step` runs; after `step` returns, the snapshot file is replaced unconditionally. Two concurrent lease events can therefore lose an event. For example, suppose the snapshot is current at shard size `N`. Process A appends lease event A (`before=N`), reads `cur` at size `N`, `_continues` returns true, projects A, and prepares a snapshot for size `N+1`. Before A writes, process B appends lease event B (`before=N+1`), rebuilds from the log, and atomically writes a snapshot containing A and B. Process A then writes its older snapshot containing only A. The hook reads only the snapshot; it is within `snapshot_max_age_s` and has the current config stamp, so it is treated as OK even though B’s lease is absent. A hook checking a glob claimed by B can then allow a conflicting write. The same unconditional failure path can also remove a concurrently written fresh snapshot. Atomic replacement prevents torn reads but does not prevent this lost-update silent pass.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/snapshot.py:192 (`apply`)

chunk_findings.detail: `_lease` checks only that `ttl_s` and `renewed_at` are finite numbers, not that they are plausible. A snapshot whose `config_stamp` matches and whose lease has `"ttl_s": -1` is accepted as `OK`; `Snapshot.live_for(holder, now)` then computes expiry as `renewed_at + -1`, so a still-live holder with `"globs": ["src/**"]` is treated as expired. A hook using that snapshot allows a conflicting write instead of returning `UNREADABLE` and failing open to the commit-time check.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce/hooksnap.py:_lease

chunk_findings.detail: `_num(data["written_at"])` accepts any finite number, including far-future timestamps, and the stale check only compares `age > limit`. For `"written_at": 9999999999` and `"max_age_s": 60`, at the current epoch `age` is negative, so `read()` returns `OK` and bypasses `[locks].snapshot_max_age_s`. A stale lease table in such a file is therefore trusted silently (for example after a clock rollback or corrupted timestamp) when it should be reported stale or unreadable and fail open.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce/hooksnap.py:read

chunk_findings.detail: `_sizes()` deliberately omits any shard whose `sh.stat()` raises `OSError`. `_continues()` then iterates only over the successfully stat’ed shards, so the critical `name == shard` check is skipped if the target shard could not be stat’ed. For example, if the shard the event was just appended to is unlinked or rotated away between `log.append` and `_continues` (so `_sizes` omits it), `_continues` can return `True` as long as every other shard matches, without ever verifying `marks[shard] == before`. It then incrementally projects only the new event onto `cur` and writes the snapshot as current, even though the snapshot may be behind the log and missing earlier events from that omitted shard. A stat failure should make the snapshot “not current” and force a rebuild, not make the missing shard invisible to the check.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases/snapshot.py:_sizes/_continues

chunk_findings.detail: The test still measures `CK.verdict` 200 times in one warm process, after imports are loaded and any module-level caches are populated. A real per-edit hook starts a fresh process and must import ddflow before this function is called; those costs are entirely outside the timed window. An implementation whose process startup/import is, say, 200 ms but whose in-process `CK.verdict` is 1 ms passes this assertion, while the actual hook violates the 30 ms p95 budget. This is the cold-start half of prior finding 9; changing the timed call from `_mine` to `CK.verdict` does not address it.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_lease_snapshot.py:test_hook_read_budget_p95_under_30_ms

chunk_findings.detail: The new assertion says “an item that ended holds nothing, whoever ended it,” but the test now passes `actor="b"` and `data={"holder":"b"}` — the same holder. The previous version passed a non-holder actor (`"a"`) with empty event data, so the suite no longer exercises a non-holder completing an item or a legacy/empty `item.completed` event clearing the lease. If the projection clears only when the actor equals the holder (or only when `data` includes a holder), all current tests still pass while a non-holder completion leaves a stale lease. This should keep a case such as `S.project(leases, "item.completed", "T", {"holder": "b"}, "a")` and assert `leases == {}`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_lease_snapshot.py:220-221
